leads_to.evidence: Fire departments hire with a high school diploma, a few months at a fire academy and usually EMT certification. A bachelor's in fire science mostly helps firefighters get promoted into officer and administrative jobs.

nearby_pair.evidence: No nearby pair was identified for this major.

school_matters.evidence: Most Fire Protection graduates go into fire service jobs, where public pay scales set pay and a degree is not needed to get hired. Graduates of the many open-admission schools earn about the same as the few more selective programs.

who_is_counted.evidence: Several large programs are online completion degrees for people already working in fire service. Some require a public safety associate degree, certification or job to get in. Campus programs alongside them take traditional students.

programs.evidence: SIU Carbondale's Public Safety Management degree, with its Fire Service Management track, requires a public safety associate degree, equivalent fire training, a license or certification, or public safety work experience to get in.

Colorado State's fire and emergency services degree is an online completion program. It strongly prefers two years of fire or EMS experience or a fire science associate degree, and most of its students already work in the field.

Waldorf's fire science administration degree is fully online and marketed to working firefighters. It has partnerships with the FDNY and the National Volunteer Fire Council, plus an applied version for experienced professionals.
Western Illinois offers this major on campus in Macomb and its Fire Administration option online, so its graduates may be a mix of new and working students. Nothing found explains the lower earnings.
The cohort is under 20 graduates, too few for a reliable figure.
Methodist University's own pages show no fire degree. Third-party listings show it awards degrees in fire and arson investigation, and nothing found explains the low earnings.
